passage: Home-visit note by Sangeeta, anganwadi worker. Gopika, five, folded her hands in namaste when I came in and said, "Namaste, Sangeeta-didi." Her grandmother told me that they do not insist on it. Instead, everyone greets each other this way each morning, and Gopika started copying it a few months ago. When I gave her a biscuit she put her hand over her heart, smiling. I noted that respect seems to be growing from warmth and repetition, not from being told to do it.

qa.q: What did Gopika say when she folded her hands?
qa.a: She said, "Namaste, Sangeeta-didi."

qa.q: What might Gopika be feeling when she places her hand over her heart after getting the biscuit?
qa.a: She seems to feel thankful and happy, since she is smiling. She could also simply be copying what she sees others do.

qa.q: What could families do to help children learn respectful greetings?
qa.a: They can greet each other warmly every day and let children copy at their own pace, as Gopika's family does.

qa.q: How does Gopika's grandmother see it?
qa.a: She sees that Gopika has learned to greet people because the family does it daily, and not because she was forced.

grounding: A preschooler folds her hands in namaste or places a hand over the heart to greet or thank, learned through warm modelling.

passage: At the village's temple courtyard, Madhav, four, saw the elderly priest and pressed his palms together, saying "Namaste, Baba." He had watched his father Shankar do the same every evening. The priest smiled and touched his head lightly, and Madhav giggled. Shankar hadn't told him to do it. Later a small boy from another village just waved. Shankar only smiled at both, and said, "Everyone has a way to say hello."

qa.q: Where did Madhav greet the priest?
qa.a: He greeted the priest in the temple courtyard.

qa.q: What might Madhav have been feeling when the priest touched his head?
qa.a: He probably felt happy and welcomed, since he giggled. He might also have felt a little shy.

qa.q: What could Shankar do if Madhav didn't want to fold his hands one evening?
qa.a: He can keep greeting people warmly himself and let Madhav join in when he wants.

qa.q: How might the priest see Madhav's namaste?
qa.a: The priest may see a small child showing respect and warmth, and answered with a smile and a gentle touch.

grounding: A preschooler folds his hands in namaste as respect learned through modelling, without being forced.

passage: Daniel's grandmother had flown to London from Pune. At the door, his mother folded her hands and said, “Namaste, Aai.” Daniel copied, pressing his palms together. Grandma's face lit up. Then his friend Elif, visiting from next door, put her right hand over her heart and bowed her head a little, the way her family greeted older people. Grandma laughed and did it back to her. Later, Daniel greeted his grandpa on a video call with both: hands together, then hand on heart.

qa.q: Where had Daniel's grandmother flown from?
qa.a: From Pune.

qa.q: What was Grandma feeling when Daniel pressed his palms together?
qa.a: She was delighted and touched that he greeted her in the way she knew. She may also have felt a bit emotional after a long journey to see him.

qa.q: What helped Daniel learn the greeting?
qa.a: He saw his mother model it warmly at the door and copied her, with no one forcing him.

qa.q: How might Elif's greeting look to Daniel's grandmother?
qa.a: She saw it as a respectful, kind gesture from another family's tradition, and happily returned it.

grounding: A preschooler learns to greet an elder with namaste by copying his mother, and a friend greets with a hand over her heart.

passage: The preschool visited the old people's home near the market. Jagdish Sir walked in first and greeted every resident with folded hands, smiling. Imran watched, then folded his hands too and said a shy “Namaste” to a lady in a shawl. She put her hand on her heart and blessed him. One girl hid behind the door. Jagdish Sir didn't push her. “You can wave, or just watch today,” he said. She waved from the doorway, and a grandpa waved back.

qa.q: What did the lady in a shawl do when Imran greeted her?
qa.a: She put her hand on her heart and blessed him.

qa.q: What was Imran feeling when he said a shy “Namaste”?
qa.a: He felt shy but wanted to join in, having watched Jagdish Sir greet everyone. After the blessing he likely felt proud.

qa.q: What was wise about how Jagdish Sir handled the girl who hid?
qa.a: He didn't force a greeting and offered a wave or watching, so respect stayed warm rather than pressured.

qa.q: What was it like for the residents to be greeted by the children?
qa.a: They likely felt happy and valued, which showed in the lady's blessing and the grandpa's wave.

grounding: A preschooler learns to greet elders with namaste through warm modelling, and a shy child is not forced.

passage: I'm Kiran, from the house across the lane. Last Sunday Chaitanya's great-grandmother came to stay. When his mother brought him out, Chaitanya hid his face in her sari. His mother didn't pull him. She just folded her hands and greeted the old lady herself. A little later I saw Chaitanya peek out, put his small hand on his chest, and bow his head. The old lady laughed and touched his head. I don't know who taught him that, but he looked pleased.

qa.q: Where did Chaitanya hide his face?
qa.a: In his mother's sari.

qa.q: What might Chaitanya have been feeling when he hid his face?
qa.a: He was probably shy with an elder he did not know well. Later, when he put his hand on his chest, he seemed pleased and more comfortable.

qa.q: Which choice by Chaitanya's mother worked, and why?
qa.a: She didn't pull him out; she greeted the elder herself, which modelled respect and let him choose his own moment.

qa.q: How might the great-grandmother see the little bow?
qa.a: She would likely feel touched and loved, as shown by her laugh and blessing. 🙂

grounding: A neighbour observes a preschooler greet an elder with a hand on his chest after his mother models respect without force.

passage:
Sunday: Dadi arrived, and Mummy pushed Alka's hands together. "Say namaste properly!" Alka pulled away and hid behind the curtain.

The next Friday: Mummy didn't push. She simply greeted Dadi warmly, hands folded, smiling. When Asif Chacha from downstairs brought sweets, she thanked him and he touched his hand to his heart. Alka watched from the sofa.

The Sunday after: Alka ran to the door, folded her hands for Dadi, then turned and put a hand on her chest for Asif Chacha. Both of them beamed.

qa.q: What did Asif Chacha bring on Friday?
qa.a: Sweets.

qa.q: Why did Alka hide behind the curtain on the first Sunday?
qa.a: She most likely felt embarrassed and upset at being pushed into a greeting, so she pulled away. She may also have been shy after not seeing Dadi for a while.

qa.q: What worked better than pushing Alka's hands together?
qa.a: Mummy simply greeted people warmly herself, so Alka could watch and copy the gestures when she was ready.

qa.q: How do Dadi and Asif Chacha feel when Alka greets them on her own?
qa.a: They beam, so they feel pleased and touched that the greeting came from her, each in their own style.

grounding: It shows a preschooler learning namaste and a hand-on-heart greeting through warm modelling rather than force.
